William Jones. A British philologist and judge in eighteenth-century India whose eighteen eighty-six proposal of a genetic relationship between Sanskrit, Greek, and Latin founded the field of comparative linguistics and launched the modern investigation into Indo-European languages. His insight that these languages shared a common ancestor revolutionised the study of language and early human history. Jones proposed in a famous address to the Asiatic Society of Bengal that Sanskrit, Greek, and Latin were descended from a common parent language, establishing the Indo-European hypothesis that would anchor all subsequent historical linguistics. He was a polymathic scholar fluent in at least thirteen languages, including Sanskrit, Persian, Arabic, and Chinese, which enabled him to perceive the deeper structural kinships that others had missed. His position as a judge in Bengal gave him access to Sanskrit texts and the opportunity to study the language deeply rather than relying on secondhand accounts. He developed the comparative method—systematic alignment of cognates—which became the empirical foundation for all subsequent historical linguistics. Though he did not live to build out the full comparative framework himself, his insight immediately inspired others to map out the entire Indo-European language family and establish the methodological principles that define comparative linguistics to this day.
